Chronology 6 — David, Solomon, and the Portrayal of God's Chosen

This chapter isolates a systematic pattern, not a single episode: the two texts portray God's chosen servants on opposite philosophies.

The Bible's text — what is actually said

  • David: adultery with Bathsheba, then the engineered death of Uriah (2 Sam 11); Nathan's trap-parable and "You are the man" (2 Sam 12); the child dies; lifelong consequences; the penitential Ps 51 ("a broken and contrite heart"). Yet David is still "a man after God's own heart" — the Bible both condemns and elevates him.
  • Solomon: in old age his foreign wives turn his heart; he builds high places for other gods (1 Kgs 11) — narrated as real apostasy.
  • The pattern is general: patriarchs, prophets, and kings shown "warts and all" — deceit, violence, idolatry, doubt.

The Qur'an's text — what is actually said

  • Dāwūd and Sulaymān are righteous prophets. The Bathsheba/ Uriah episode is absent; Q 38:21–25 (the two litigants) has Dāwūd realise "We had tried him", ask forgiveness, and be forgiven — but no adultery or murder is narrated (classical exegetes were themselves uneasy about what the sin was, and largely purged the Bathsheba material that had entered early tafsīr as isrāʾīliyyāt).
  • Sulaymān is "an excellent servant" (Q 38:30); his alleged idolatry is not affirmed (Q 2:102 shifts blame to the devils).
  • Governing doctrine: *prophetic impeccability (ʿiṣma)*.

The symmetry the popular argument hides

The neat "Bible: sinful prophets / Qurʾan: sinless prophets" contrast is partly false on the Qurʾan's own text — and symmetry requires saying so (cf. how cap. 11 showed Ezek 18 sits inside the Bible against original sin):

  • The Qurʾan itself shows prophets erring and seeking forgiveness: Adam (Q 7:23); Mūsā after killing the Egyptian — "my Lord, I have wronged myself, forgive me" (Q 28:16); Yūnus — "I have been of the wrongdoers" (Q 21:87); Dāwūd asking forgiveness (Q 38:24); and Muhammad himself addressed "ask forgiveness for your sin" (Q 47:19; 48:2; the ʿAbasa rebuke, Q 80:1–10).
  • So ʿiṣma (especially its strong form) is, in part, a later harmonising doctrine, not a flat Qurʾanic given. The real divergence is therefore Bible vs. developed Islamic doctrine more than Bible vs. Qurʾanic text — exactly the kind of precision the dossier applied to the Christian side.

Collision

This is the clearest "different by design" divergence in the dossier:

BibleQur'an
Portrayal of the chosenflawed, sinning humansmorally elevated, protected
David's adultery/murdernarrated and condemnednot narrated
Solomon's idolatrynarrateddenied/deflected
Governing doctrinegrace despite sin'isma (impeccability)

Logic — and why it matters methodologically

  • The Bible's embarrassing detail engages the criterion of embarrassment: a tradition that damages its own heroes is less likely to be invented — a recognised neutral-historian tool, not a Christian apologetic invention. Caveat: the criterion is suggestive, not absolute — the unflattering detail also serves the Bible's own grace theme, so it is not pure raw history either.
  • Strong ʿiṣma is a theological axiom about what befits a prophet — not falsifiable — and, as shown above, is in tension with the Qurʾan's own text (prophets repent). So the cleanest framing is Bible-narrative vs. later-doctrine, with the Qurʾanic text sitting nearer the Bible than the doctrine admits.
  • Both systems are internally coherent; they are *different kinds of claim* — one invites historical assessment, the other states (and then harmonises toward) a doctrine.

Arbiter verdict — the chosen

Present. Bible: fallible servants saved by grace. Qur'an: protected servants befitting revelation.

Weigh.

  • Methodological weight, Bible: the criterion of embarrassment is a standard, neutral historiographic tool and favours the non-invention of the unflattering accounts.
  • Theological axiom, Qur'an: 'isma is coherent as doctrine but contributes no historical evidence; it explains the divergence rather than evidencing it.
  • Symmetry check: this is not a corruption proof against either — it is a difference of portrayal philosophy.

Judge. On historical-evidentiary value: a measured advantage Bible — the criterion of embarrassment makes its self-damaging detail harder to dismiss as invention, though the criterion is suggestive, not decisive. On the contrast itself: the popular "sinful vs. sinless prophets" framing is partly false — the Qurʾanic text also has prophets repent; the sharp divergence is really *Bible vs. the developed ʿiṣma doctrine, with the Qurʾan's own wording closer to the Bible than later theology concedes (symmetry with the Ezek 18 point in cap. 11). Whether revelation should* embarrass or protect its heroes remains the non-arbitrable value premise (Methodology §5). Still the dossier's tidiest case of "different by design, not by corruption" — now with the added precision that the design is doctrinal, layered over a text that is less divergent than the slogans suggest.
